fields.meta_title: Artist Landing Page Builder for Musicians | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an artist landing page from a prompt. See four music examples: a single release, tour dates, booking requests, and session dates.
fields.h1: Build an Artist Landing Page That Turns Listeners Into Fans
fields.hero_description: Get an artist landing page built from one prompt, with your music up front and every fan email saved to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Behind the Music
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the page fans land on and the database that remembers everyone who signs up or asks to book you.
fields.feature_1:
A page written from your description

Tell Emergent who you are, what is out now, and what a fan should do next, and it builds the page, the signup, and the forms. A new single next month takes one more prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Fan emails in a database you own

The app saves every signup to a database you own, with the email, the city, and where the fan found you. If you ever switch mailing tools, the whole list stays with you.
fields.feature_3:
An alert for the requests that pay

Name the requests you want to hear about at once, such as a wedding date or a festival slot, and the app sends you an email, Slack, or in-app alert with the details in it.
fields.feature_4:
Connected to the tools you already run

Built apps connect to any tool with an API. Signups can sync out to the email tool you use. Your calendar can sync in, which keeps the page and your schedule in step.
fields.feature_5:
Your band name as the address

Publish the page on a custom domain such as yourbandname.com; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. A short address is easy to say from the stage.
fields.feature_6:
Free to publish, yours to export

The free tier covers building and publishing your page. On paid plans, Emergent exports the full code to your GitHub repository, so a developer friend can keep working on it.

fields.tab_content_1:
Her video link brought in 268 of 412 signups

Nadia Ferro put out her single Paper Lanterns with a release page that has her streaming links and an email signup. The app saves each signup with the link the fan came from. Of 412 signups in release week, 268 came from the link in her video description and 144 from her Instagram bio.
fields.tab_content_2:
Adding a Denver date emailed all 87 Denver fans

Fans on Low Orchard's tour page type their city when they sign up, and the app keeps both in the band's fan table. On March 3 the band added a Denver show, and the app emailed all 87 fans who had entered Denver, with the date, the venue, and the ticket link.
fields.tab_content_3:
Gigs over $2,000 land with the manager, Priya

Every booking request the Wendell Ames Trio gets asks for the date, the event type, and the budget. A request over $2,000 goes to their manager, Priya Castellanos, as an email with the answers in it, and smaller ones go to Wendell's own list. In October, 9 of 31 requests went to Priya and the other 22 to Wendell.
fields.tab_content_4:
Her form offers 11 open days in April

Tess Okonkwo plays drums on other people's records, and producers book her through a request form on her page. The app reads free/busy information from her Google Calendar through its API, so the form offers only the days she is free. In April, 19 of 30 days were booked, leaving 11 open.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Artist Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps take an artist landing page from one clear job to a tested page that saves every fan and booking request.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Describe the page in one prompt
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Ask for a city with the email
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide what a fan should do today: stream the new single, join the list for tour news, or ask about a booking. Lead with that action, and move everything else lower down or off the page.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Open the page on the record fans are hearing about now, with the cover art and your streaming links next to it. Older releases can sit in a short list further down the page.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Name the sections, the fields on each form, and what happens after someone submits: which table keeps the row and who gets an alert. Emergent builds the page and its database from that prompt.
fields.howto_step_4_des: One extra field lets you write to the fans near a new show instead of the whole list. Stop at those two fields: a short signup fits on a phone screen without scrolling.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Give each place you share the page its own tagged link, such as ?from=video or ?from=bio, and ask in your prompt for each signup to be saved with its tag. After a release, compare the counts.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Sign up from your own phone with a test city, then send one booking request. Check that both rows land in the table and that the alert reaches you before the address goes in your bio.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Swap the top for the next record
fields.howto_step_7_des: When the next single is out, one more prompt moves it to the top and pushes the last one into the older list. Read the signup counts by tag that same week, and post more where fans came from.

faq_plan.q: What is the best free landing page for music?
faq_plan.ref: What is the best free landing page for music?

prov.original: What is the best free landing page for music?

faq_plan.a: The best free landing page for music is one you can publish at no cost that keeps every fan email in a list you control. Before you pick one, check that it holds your streaming links and a signup, and that you can change the page the week your next song comes out. Test it by signing up yourself from a phone.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an artist landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe it to Emergent's AI landing page builder in plain words: your name, what is out now, the forms you want, and what should happen to each submission. From that prompt, Emergent builds the page and the tables behind its forms, and another prompt changes either one. Write the prompt around one action, such as joining the list for tour news, and keep the rest short.

faq_plan.q: What do good artist landing page examples have in common?
faq_plan.a: They lead with one release and one action, and every other part of the page supports it. The four examples on this page each do a job after the click. One saves each signup with its source, one emails fans by city, one routes booking requests by budget, and one offers only free dates.

faq_plan.q: When do music landing page templates fall short?
faq_plan.a: They fall short when the page has to act on each submission, such as sending booking requests over a set budget to your manager. Use a template when a layout is all you need. If you teach lessons on the side, give them a separate course landing page so students and fans each land on the page meant for them.

faq_plan.q: What should go at the top of a musician landing page?
faq_plan.a: Put your name, your newest release with its streaming links, and one button for the action you want most. A fan who scrolls no further should still be able to play the song and join your list. Leave the full discography and press quotes for further down the page.

faq_plan.q: How do I collect fan emails on an artist landing page?
faq_plan.a: Place a short signup right under your streaming links, ask for the email and the city, and tell fans in one line what they get, such as first word on shows near them. An app built on Emergent can sync each new signup to the email tool you send from, through that tool's API.

faq_plan.q: Does each new single need its own artist landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes, while you are promoting it: one page per release keeps that record's links and signup counts together. If you also write, give each title its own book landing page. When the campaign ends, link the old page to your main artist page and keep its signups in the same fan table.

faq_plan.q: Can I put a music landing page on my own domain?
faq_plan.a: Yes: a custom domain is included in Emergent and uses credits, and the page can then sit at your band or artist name. Pick an address you can say once from a stage and spell on a poster, and keep the same one for every release so fans learn where to look.

faq_plan.q: How do I list tour dates on an artist landing page?
faq_plan.a: List each show by date and city, with the venue and a ticket link, nearest date first. Take past shows off the list the morning after, and mark sold-out dates instead of deleting them. If you ask fans for their city at signup, a new date can go straight to the people who live there.

faq_plan.q: How is an artist landing page for bookings different from one for fans?
faq_plan.a: It speaks to a different reader. A fan page asks a listener for an email, while a booking page speaks to the person paying for the night, which makes it closer to a b2b landing page. Show your set lengths and a short live clip, and have the request form ask for the night, the kind of event, and the budget.

plan.angle: The searches here want a music artist's page, and the top results are link-in-bio tools and example galleries that stop at a row of streaming buttons. This page shows four musicians whose page does a job after the click, each built from a prompt: a singer-songwriter's release page that saves each signup with the link it came from, a band's tour page that emails fans when a show is added in their city, a jazz trio's booking form that sends large gigs to the manager, and a session drummer's request form that only offers open dates. It stays on music artists, leaving visual art portfolios to the portfolio page, and the FAQ covers the free option, the build, examples, templates, what goes on top, separate release pages, fan emails, booking pages and an own address.
